title: The man with the finger garland
hookLine: Angulimala, a killer on the forest road, sees the Buddha walking alone toward him (MN 86)

cards: Some roads people simply stop using. Too dangerous after dark, or at all. In the kingdom of Kosala, in the Buddha's time, there was a whole forest like that.
Villages near it had emptied out. Somewhere on that road lived a man the old sutta calls cruel, with bloody hands, without mercy for any living thing.
He killed people who passed, cut a finger from each one, and wore them strung around his neck. So people called him Angulimala: finger garland.
One morning, after his alms round, the Buddha puts his things away and starts walking down that road.

teach.b: The sutta is short on drama and long on quiet, which makes it more frightening. People working in the fields see him heading for the forest and call out. Don't take that road, monk.
Angulimala is on it. Groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty men have gone down it together, and they've all fallen to him.
The Buddha doesn't answer. He walks on. They warn him a second time, then a third.
He walks on, in silence. That silence isn't bravado. He doesn't lecture the farmers or boast.
And he isn't reckless in the ordinary way, because he knows exactly who is on that road.
He simply walks, steady, at an ordinary pace, the way you'd walk to the corner store. Then Angulimala sees him: a lone monk, unarmed, walking into his forest. The sutta gives us his thought.
Amazing. Groups of forty men come down this road and fall, and this monk comes alone, with no one beside him, as if something were driving him here.
So he takes up his sword and shield, his bow and quiver, and starts after him. i'll stop the story there, with a killer running and a monk walking.
Tomorrow, the meeting. Later commentaries tell how this man came to be what he was: once a gifted student named Ahimsaka, which means harmless, turned by a jealous plot and a cruel teacher's demand.
The sutta itself doesn't tell that part. It only tells us the Buddha walked toward someone everyone else had given up on.

how: Buddhists retell the story of Angulimala as a story of how a person can change, in temples, in schools, and in some prison chaplaincy work.

o: a string of prayer beads worn around a monk's neck
a ring a new monk is given at his ordination
finger garland, the name of a killer on a forest road

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: harmless, his name in the commentaries
the kingdom where the road ran

s: the Buddha answered the farmers' warnings with a speech
he walked on in silence, three times.
Angulimala's first name, in later commentaries, meant harmless
Ahimsaka. the sutta itself doesn't tell his backstory.
the Buddha didn't know who was on the road
the farmers told him exactly who was there, three times.

games.q: you're walking toward a forest. farmers shout that a killer is on the road, and forty armed men have fallen there. what do you do?
o: wait for soldiers to come with you.
games.why: the Buddha walks on, three warnings, three times, at an ordinary pace, toward the man everyone else had given up on.

practice: Bring to mind something small you've been avoiding: a phone call, a person, an email sitting unopened. Picture yourself walking toward it at an ordinary pace, not running at it, not rushing past.
Where your body tightens, breathe into that spot, and keep walking in your mind, one steady step at a time.

wordCard.voice: Angulimala. The killer of the forest road in Kosala, toward whom the Buddha walked, alone and steady, wearing a garland of fingers.

orig.note: Pali: finger garland. Anguli (finger) and mala (garland).

carryVoice: Your line: walk on. Three warnings, and he answered none of them. See you tomorrow.
